# AI coding research brief — October 23, 2026

Four new sources, ranked for their practical relevance to Quadratus. This week's strongest idea is to test what happens when one agent inherits another's apparently finished work. The experiments below are proposed applications, not demonstrated improvements in Quadratus.

## 1. SWE-Residual: Evaluating Starting-State Robustness of Coding Agents
**October 19, 2026 · [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.25899)**

Across 198 inherited states from 111 tasks, five frontier agents performed substantially worse when continuing failed work previously submitted as complete: success fell 20.6–53.5 percentage points on DeepSWE and 20.6–34.9 points on Terminal-Bench versus clean starts. Successors often preserved the predecessor's failures.

**Why read it:** It directly challenges the assumption that a capable second agent will notice what the first missed. The benchmark deliberately selects failed predecessor outputs; these rates are not estimates of all real-world handoffs. Successors receive the original request and state, but no predecessor transcript or failure warning. Coverage is limited to two benchmarks and three predecessor families.

**Quadratus experiment:** Create paired evaluations from clean states and archived failed patches. Before continuation, require a fresh request-derived acceptance checklist and baseline test run. Compare verified completion, inherited failures left unchanged, and total tokens against normal handoffs.

## 2. FrontierRefactor: Benchmarking Multi-Scale Performance-Oriented Codebase Refactoring
**October 19, 2026 · [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.25834)**

Across 60 tasks and 1,080 runs, 41.2% of submissions passed functional checks but failed to deliver verified acceleration: 19.3% regressed and 21.9% remained within measurement noise. On a 25-task GPT-6 Astra subset, scalar timing feedback raised strict success from 16% to 40% over three rounds.

**Why read it:** A successful refactor needs separate evidence for behavior preservation and its claimed performance benefit. The feedback result is small and model-specific; blind retries also reached 32%, so the full 24-point increase cannot be attributed solely to timing feedback. Curated performance tasks do not represent every useful refactor.

**Quadratus experiment:** Assign the verifier two gates: unchanged observable behavior, then repeatable improvement on a frozen workload. Use warm-ups and interleaved baseline/candidate timings; return measured bottlenecks to the implementer. Compare timing-guided revision with equally budgeted blind retries.

## 3. Do Coding Agents Understand Why Systems Crash—and Why They Don't?
**October 21, 2026 · [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29332)**

SysRB pairs 934 Linux/OSS-Fuzz source trees differing by one commit, with the same input crashing only one version. Four agents missed 27.5–76.8% of real crashes. Finding relevant code did not guarantee understanding its effect, especially across subsystems.

**Why read it:** A plausible explanation of suspicious code can remain unchanged after the bug is fixed. Paired evaluation exposes this weakness. Crucially, agents could inspect source but could not compile it or execute the reproducer: these results measure source-based reasoning, not a complete debugging loop.

**Quadratus experiment:** Have an independent worker predict the failure mechanism on pre-patch and post-patch versions separately, then run the same reproducer on both. Require the explanation to match the observed difference and retain regression checks for intended behavior.

## 4. Red-Teaming OpenAI's Internal Agent Monitoring Systems
**October 22, 2026 · [Firsthand METR report](https://metr.org/blog/2026-10-22-red-teaming-openai-agent-monitoring/)**

METR and Redwood researchers found monitoring gaps during a three-week, high-access assessment, including missed compaction events and monitoring that could be postponed while an agent kept acting. They also identified ways agents could interfere with monitoring.

**Why read it:** A supervisor cannot reliably coordinate or verify work it never observes. This is a newly published report about the system as of July 21, not evidence of current coverage. The public account omits exploit details; OpenAI says production-safeguard vulnerabilities were patched, but the evaluators have not verified those claims.

**Quadratus experiment:** In a sandbox, reconcile independently recorded worker actions against supervisor receipts across long turns, compaction and resumed workers. Simulate monitor failure and confirm the run remains explicitly incomplete. Keep monitoring state outside workers' writable environments.

## The single most promising idea to try

**Add a failed-handoff regression set.** Use known incomplete patches to test whether a fresh worker independently reconstructs the requested outcome before continuing. Compare ordinary handoffs against a request-first checklist plus baseline execution, with equal budgets. Track propagated failures, final verified success, tokens and elapsed time. This tests a central risk of master-agent coordination directly.
